questions.prompt: Two application VMs must not both restart in the same planned platform-maintenance batch. Which availability-set concept addresses this requirement?

options.text: Different update domains
options.explanation: Update domains group VMs that can restart together; spreading these VMs across them separates their planned-maintenance batches.

options.text: Only different fault domains
options.explanation: Fault domains reduce shared power or network hardware exposure; update domains define planned-maintenance restart groups.

options.text: The same update domain
options.explanation: VMs in the same update domain can restart together, which conflicts with the requirement.

options.text: A larger VM size
options.explanation: A larger size changes capacity, not the update-domain grouping that controls these maintenance batches.

questions.prompt: An application has replicated VM instances and must withstand the loss of one datacenter within a supported region. Which placement best meets this goal?

options.text: Place every instance in one availability zone
options.explanation: One zone leaves the instances exposed to that zone's datacenter failure.

options.text: Distribute instances across availability zones
options.explanation: Zones are physically separate locations with independent power, cooling and networking; replicated instances in other zones can serve the workload.

options.text: Increase the size of one VM
options.explanation: Additional CPU or memory does not place another application instance in a separate physical zone.

options.text: Use one availability set as the entire datacenter-failure solution
options.explanation: Availability sets reduce shared hardware and maintenance exposure but are not the cross-datacenter placement provided by zones.

questions.prompt: A workload changes from two VM instances to five, while keeping each VM size unchanged. What type of scaling occurred?

options.text: Vertical scale up
options.explanation: Vertical scaling changes each VM's size, which remained unchanged here.

options.text: Horizontal scale in
options.explanation: Scale in removes instances; this change added three.

options.text: Horizontal scale out
options.explanation: Horizontal scaling changes instance count; adding instances is scale out.

options.text: Vertical scale down
options.explanation: Scale down reduces VM size; it does not describe an increase in instance count.

questions.prompt: A team needs a scale set whose VMs can use different images and sizes. Which orchestration mode should it choose when creating the set?

options.text: Uniform
options.explanation: Uniform uses a shared base image and configuration, so it does not meet the requested mixed-configuration model.

options.text: An availability set instead of an orchestration mode
options.explanation: Availability sets provide placement protection; they are not a scale-set orchestration mode.

options.text: A deployment slot
options.explanation: Deployment slots stage App Service releases; they do not define scale-set VM orchestration.

options.text: Flexible
options.explanation: Flexible orchestration allows differing VM images, sizes and configurations within one scale set.

questions.prompt: CPU load stays high during business hours and drops for hours overnight. Which autoscale design addresses both performance and unnecessary capacity?

options.text: Scale out for sustained high load and scale in for sustained low load
options.explanation: Paired rules add instances when demand requires them and remove unnecessary instances after demand falls.

options.text: Configure only scale-out rules
options.explanation: This can add capacity under load but provides no corresponding rule to remove it overnight.

options.text: Scale in whenever CPU rises
options.explanation: Removing instances during sustained high demand moves capacity in the wrong direction.

options.text: Use one fixed instance count and no autoscale
options.explanation: Fixed capacity does not automatically respond to the stated sustained changes in demand.

questions.prompt: A scale-set web application needs HTTP path routing and TLS termination at its traffic distributor. Which service matches the layer-seven requirement?

options.text: Azure Load Balancer alone
options.explanation: Load Balancer distributes layer-four traffic; it does not provide the requested HTTP path routing and TLS termination.

options.text: Azure Application Gateway
options.explanation: Application Gateway provides layer-seven routing and TLS termination for the stated web traffic.

options.text: An availability set
options.explanation: An availability set controls VM placement, not HTTP routing or TLS termination.

options.text: An autoscale schedule
options.explanation: A schedule changes instance capacity at planned times; it does not route requests or terminate TLS.

questions.prompt: Two web apps share an App Service plan. A new resource-intensive app could exhaust its remaining capacity and needs independent scaling. What is the most appropriate plan design?

options.text: Add it to the existing plan without checking capacity
options.explanation: Apps share plan resources, so unchecked additional demand can affect existing apps.

options.text: Place the new app in a separate plan
options.explanation: A separate plan provides a separate compute and scaling boundary rather than burdening the existing apps' shared capacity.

options.text: Keep all three apps in the same plan and rely only on plan-level autoscale
options.explanation: Plan-level autoscale changes shared plan capacity; it does not give the resource-intensive app its own independent compute and scaling boundary.

options.text: Add the new app to the same plan because apps never compete for capacity
options.explanation: Apps share plan compute resources, so the new app can affect the other apps when capacity is overloaded.

questions.prompt: A developer uses the Free App Service tier and now needs multiple instances. Can the existing Free tier simply scale out?

options.text: Yes; all App Service tiers support additional instances
options.explanation: The pricing lesson explicitly excludes scale out for Free and Shared.

options.text: Yes; adding another deployment slot increases Free-tier instances
options.explanation: Slots are deployment environments on supported tiers, not a way to bypass the Free tier's scaling limit.

options.text: No; choose a tier that supports scale out
options.explanation: Free and Shared use shared compute with CPU quotas and cannot scale out.

options.text: No; App Service never supports scale out
options.explanation: Dedicated tiers support scale out within their tier limits; the restriction here is the Free tier.

questions.prompt: A web app needs more memory per worker, rather than additional workers of the same size. Which change addresses that requirement?

options.text: Scale out with the current worker size
options.explanation: Scale out adds workers but does not increase the memory of each worker.

options.text: Add a scale-in rule
options.explanation: Scale in removes workers; it does not increase per-worker memory.

options.text: Add more apps to the same worker size
options.explanation: More apps sharing the same workers do not increase memory available per worker and can increase resource contention.

options.text: Scale up the App Service plan
options.explanation: Scale up changes tier or instance size to obtain more per-instance CPU, memory or features.

questions.prompt: An App Service plan is scaled out from two workers to four. Its app uses Azure SQL Database. Which dependency assumption must the administrator avoid?

options.text: Assuming Azure SQL automatically gains capacity with the plan
options.explanation: Plan scaling affects App Service compute; dependent databases and storage require their own capacity decisions.

options.text: Expecting the plan to add App Service workers
options.explanation: Adding App Service instances is exactly what scale out does.

options.text: Checking whether the selected tier supports four workers
options.explanation: Tier limits constrain scale out, so this is a necessary capacity check.

options.text: Reviewing the other apps sharing the plan
options.explanation: Plan scaling can affect shared apps, so reviewing them is appropriate.

questions.prompt: A Premium v3 app should add capacity every weekday before a predictable morning rush using a custom schedule. Which feature fits?

options.text: Automatic scaling with a custom schedule rule
options.explanation: App Service automatic scaling is HTTP-traffic-driven and does not use custom autoscale schedule rules.

options.text: Rule-based autoscale with a scheduled profile
options.explanation: Autoscale supports schedule-based profiles and custom rules for predictable demand.

options.text: A manual fixed instance count with no schedule
options.explanation: A fixed manual count cannot perform the requested recurring capacity change automatically.

options.text: Use only a CPU threshold and no scheduled profile
options.explanation: A CPU rule reacts to measured demand; the stated goal is scheduled capacity before the known rush.

questions.prompt: An autoscale profile has minimum 2, maximum 8 and default 4 instances. Metrics become unavailable while 6 instances run. How does the fallback-to-default behavior apply?

options.text: It must immediately scale in to exactly 4
options.explanation: The default is not an instruction to scale in when metrics are unavailable.

options.text: It must immediately scale out to the maximum 8
options.explanation: Maximum bounds capacity; it is not the missing-metrics fallback target.

options.text: It does not scale in from 6 to the default 4
options.explanation: Default fallback scales out only when current capacity is below the default; it does not reduce a higher current count to default.

options.text: It must remove every instance
options.explanation: The minimum and fallback behavior do not direct the service to zero instances here.

questions.prompt: A supported App Service app runs a continuous WebJob. Which setting keeps the app loaded even when incoming traffic is idle?

options.text: Session affinity
options.explanation: Session affinity sends a client to the same instance during its session; it does not keep an idle app loaded.

options.text: HTTPS Only
options.explanation: HTTPS Only redirects HTTP to HTTPS; it does not keep the app active for a continuous WebJob.

options.text: Always On
options.explanation: Always On keeps the app loaded during idle periods and is required for continuous or CRON-triggered WebJobs.

options.text: A custom domain
options.explanation: A custom domain changes the app's public name, not its idle-loading behavior.

questions.prompt: A web app on a supported Standard plan needs to validate a release before replacing production. Which workflow matches the module?

options.text: Deploy untested content directly to production first
options.explanation: This replaces production before the requested preproduction validation.

options.text: Swap the empty staging slot before deploying and testing the release
options.explanation: The required workflow deploys and validates the release before exchanging content with production.

options.text: Treat the staging slot as an offline backup file
options.explanation: A deployment slot is a live app with its own hostname, not a backup archive.

options.text: Deploy to a staging slot, validate it, then swap
options.explanation: A live staging slot permits validation before its content and eligible configuration are exchanged with production.

questions.prompt: Staging and production use different database connection strings. Each string must remain with its own slot after a content swap. What should you configure?

options.text: Mark each connection string as a deployment-slot setting
options.explanation: Slot-specific connection strings remain attached to their slots when app content swaps.

options.text: Leave both strings as ordinary swappable settings
options.explanation: Eligible ordinary settings can move with content, which would violate the stated requirement.

options.text: Rename the slots without marking the connection strings
options.explanation: Slot names alone do not make a connection string slot-specific.

options.text: Copy the production string into staging permanently
options.explanation: That removes the required separation between staging and production databases.

questions.prompt: An app has a public home page and protected account pages. Its own code handles authorization. Which built-in authentication behavior preserves access for anonymous home-page visitors?

options.text: Require authentication for every request
options.explanation: That also restricts unauthenticated requests to the public home page.

options.text: Allow anonymous requests and let app code authorize protected routes
options.explanation: This permits unauthenticated traffic to reach app code, where the app can protect the appropriate routes.

options.text: Turn on HTTPS Only as the authorization policy
options.explanation: HTTPS secures transport; it does not distinguish anonymous public routes from protected account routes.

options.text: Use session affinity instead of authorization
options.explanation: Affinity selects an instance for a client session; it is not access control.

questions.prompt: You control www.example.net and its DNS provider supports CNAME records. You want the mapping to follow the app hostname even if its underlying IP changes. Which record fits?

options.text: An A record containing the current app IP
options.explanation: An A record fixes the mapping to that address and needs updating if it changes.

options.text: A connection string containing the domain
options.explanation: Connection strings configure application dependencies, not public DNS hostname mapping.

options.text: A CNAME to the App Service hostname
options.explanation: CNAME maps one hostname to another, so it follows resolution of the target when the target IP changes.

options.text: A deployment-slot setting containing the domain
options.explanation: A slot setting alone creates no DNS mapping; custom-domain validation and configuration are still required.

questions.prompt: Requests became slow after an app began calling an external API. Which Application Insights data best tests whether that API is contributing to the delay?

options.text: Only incoming request counts, ignoring dependency telemetry
options.explanation: Request counts show overall traffic but do not isolate response times and failures of the external API calls.

options.text: Only the app's exception count, ignoring successful but slow calls
options.explanation: Exceptions can reveal failures, but dependency timings are needed to investigate successful calls that are slow.

options.text: Only the configured runtime version
options.explanation: The runtime version is configuration, not measured latency or failures of the external API.

options.text: Dependency response times and failure rates
options.explanation: Dependency telemetry reveals latency and failures in calls to external services.

questions.prompt: A team compares typical process-isolated containers with full virtual machines. Which operating-system distinction is accurate?

options.text: Every process-isolated container boots its own complete guest kernel
options.explanation: That describes the full-VM model, not typical process-isolated containers.

options.text: Virtual machines cannot run different guest operating systems
options.explanation: Hardware virtualization allows separate guest OS instances; VMs are not restricted to one shared guest kernel.

options.text: Container images contain no application runtime or libraries
options.explanation: Images package application code and its runtime dependencies for consistent deployment.

options.text: Containers share a host kernel; each VM runs a guest OS and kernel
options.explanation: Typical process-isolated containers virtualize an OS environment, while VMs virtualize hardware for a full guest operating system.

questions.prompt: A Linux web application and its logging sidecar must share a lifecycle and local network in Azure Container Instances. Which resource should contain them?

options.text: One multi-container group
options.explanation: Containers in a group share lifecycle, resources, local networking and storage volumes; multi-container groups support Linux.

options.text: Two unrelated container groups
options.explanation: Separate groups do not provide the same shared group lifecycle and local-network boundary.

options.text: One Windows multi-container group
options.explanation: ACI Windows groups support a single container; this Linux sidecar design uses a Linux multi-container group.

options.text: An App Service deployment slot
options.explanation: A slot stages an App Service release; it is not an ACI container group.

questions.prompt: An ACI workload needs persistent data through an Azure Files volume mount. Which container operating system supports that mount?

options.text: Windows only
options.explanation: ACI can run Windows containers, but the Azure Files mount feature is not supported for them.

options.text: Linux
options.explanation: ACI Azure Files volume mounts are supported for Linux containers.

options.text: Both Windows and Linux with no platform restriction
options.explanation: General ACI OS support does not mean every feature, including Azure Files mounts, supports both.

options.text: Neither; ACI cannot mount persistent storage
options.explanation: Linux ACI groups can mount Azure Files, so persistent storage is supported within that platform restriction.

questions.prompt: A publicly exposed ACI container listens on TCP 8080. How should the deployment expose that port to external clients?

options.text: Expose 8080 only on the container
options.explanation: A container port alone does not expose it on the group's public IP address.

options.text: Expose 8080 only at group level while the container listens elsewhere
options.explanation: The group-level port must correspond to a listening container port; ACI does not map it to an arbitrary different port.

options.text: Expose 8080 at both the group IP address and the container
options.explanation: External access requires a group-level exposed port and a container listening on that port; ACI has no port mapping.

options.text: Map public 80 to container 8080 using ACI port mapping
options.explanation: ACI containers share a port namespace and do not support this port-mapping mechanism.

questions.prompt: An existing ACI group needs a different CPU and memory allocation. Which lifecycle change is required for those resource changes?

options.text: Change CPU and memory through an in-place group update
options.explanation: These resource properties are excluded from supported in-place updates.

options.text: Restart the group without changing its deployment
options.explanation: Restarting the existing allocation does not establish a new CPU or memory request.

options.text: Update only the container image to request a larger allocation
options.explanation: Image changes are distinct from group CPU and memory resource allocation, which requires group recreation.

options.text: Delete and recreate the group with the new allocation
options.explanation: ACI does not support updating CPU or memory resource allocation in place; recreate the group and account for its connectivity changes.

questions.prompt: A team wants managed microservices with HTTP/event-driven scaling and traffic splitting, without direct Kubernetes API access. Which service best fits the described requirement?

options.text: Azure Container Apps
options.explanation: Container Apps supplies managed serverless microservices, scaling and traffic splitting while abstracting the underlying Kubernetes platform.

options.text: Azure Container Instances as the complete microservices orchestration layer
options.explanation: ACI suits isolated containers but does not provide the described managed Container Apps microservices feature set.

options.text: Azure Kubernetes Service because direct Kubernetes access is required
options.explanation: The scenario explicitly avoids direct Kubernetes API management; Container Apps better matches the desired abstraction.

options.text: An availability set of VMs alone
options.explanation: An availability set supplies VM placement protection, not managed container traffic splitting and event-driven scaling.

questions.prompt: A business can tolerate 30 minutes of lost data and requires service restoration within 2 hours. Which recovery objectives describe those limits?

options.text: RPO 30 minutes; RTO 2 hours
options.explanation: RPO expresses tolerable data loss in time; RTO expresses the target service-restoration time.

options.text: RTO 30 minutes; RPO 2 hours
options.explanation: This reverses the definitions of data-loss tolerance and restoration-time target.

options.text: RPO 2 hours; RTO 2 hours
options.explanation: The stated data-loss tolerance is 30 minutes, not 2 hours.

options.text: RPO 30 minutes; RTO 30 minutes
options.explanation: The restoration target is 2 hours; the 30-minute value describes data-loss tolerance.

questions.prompt: An administrator needs to back up supported files, folders and system state from an on-premises Windows server directly to Azure. Which agent matches this scope?

options.text: Azure Monitor Agent
options.explanation: Azure Monitor Agent collects monitoring telemetry; it is not the backup agent for this Windows data scope.

options.text: Microsoft Azure Recovery Services (MARS) agent
options.explanation: MARS supports direct Azure backup of supported Windows files, folders and system state.

options.text: The Azure VM backup extension as the on-premises agent
options.explanation: The VM extension supports Azure VM backup; the stated machine is an on-premises Windows server.

options.text: Dependency Agent
options.explanation: Dependency Agent concerns VM dependency monitoring, not backup of Windows files, folders or system state.

questions.prompt: After an initial full backup, how do subsequent incremental backups reduce the amount of protected data transferred?

options.text: Always transfer every protected block again
options.explanation: That describes repeated full data transfer rather than the incremental approach.

options.text: Transfer only blocks that have never changed
options.explanation: Incremental backups transfer changed blocks, rather than selecting blocks precisely because they did not change.

options.text: Transfer blocks changed since the previous backup
options.explanation: Incremental backups focus on changed data blocks after the initial full copy.

options.text: Stop transferring changes until a restore is requested
options.explanation: Incremental backups capture changes during backup, not for the first time during restore.

questions.prompt: An administrator must control both when scheduled backups run and how long their recovery points are retained. Which configuration provides these controls?

options.text: A retention value without a backup schedule
options.explanation: Retention determines how long points are kept; a policy also defines when scheduled backups run.

options.text: A backup schedule without retention settings
options.explanation: Timing alone does not define how long recovery points are kept; the requirement needs both policy controls.

options.text: A recovery time objective alone
options.explanation: RTO is a target for restoring service, not the configured backup schedule and retention policy.

options.text: A backup policy
options.explanation: Backup policies define backup schedule and recovery-point retention for the protected workload.

questions.prompt: A supported workload has old recovery points kept mainly for long-term compliance and rarely accessed. Which backup storage tier is designed for that scenario?

options.text: Archive tier, where the workload and recovery points are supported
options.explanation: Archive storage targets infrequently accessed long-term recovery points; eligibility must be checked for the workload.

options.text: Snapshot tier as the universal long-term compliance tier
options.explanation: Snapshot storage is near the source for recovery and is not the archive purpose described here.

options.text: Vault-standard because every recovery point is automatically archived
options.explanation: Vault-standard stores an isolated online copy; it is not synonymous with the archive tier for supported long-term points.

options.text: A backup policy with no storage-tier decision
options.explanation: Policies establish protection settings, but do not eliminate the need to choose a supported storage tier for the described long-term points.

questions.prompt: An auditor unexpectedly requests a recovery point retained longer than the usual scheduled-policy period. What does the module identify as an option?

options.text: Assume every on-demand backup must use the scheduled retention unchanged
options.explanation: The lesson explicitly allows custom on-demand retention.

options.text: Run an on-demand backup with its own supported retention setting
options.explanation: On-demand backups can use specific retention settings independent of the scheduled-policy retention.

options.text: Disable scheduled backups to make existing points permanent
options.explanation: Disabling a schedule does not establish the requested retention for a new recovery point.

options.text: Change only the VM size
options.explanation: Compute capacity does not set backup retention.

questions.prompt: A VM owner wants recovery points for an earlier state after accidental data corruption. Which service matches this primary requirement?

options.text: Azure Site Recovery as a substitute for retained backup history
options.explanation: Site Recovery replicates workloads and coordinates failover; it is not a substitute for the requested backup retention strategy.

options.text: Azure Backup
options.explanation: Azure Backup retains recovery points for restoring an earlier data state after loss or corruption.

options.text: A VM availability set alone
options.explanation: Availability sets reduce shared infrastructure failures but do not retain earlier versions of corrupted data.

options.text: Azure Monitor alerts alone
options.explanation: Alerts can signal conditions but do not create the requested backup recovery points.

questions.prompt: Where are an Azure VM's backup policy and recovery points managed in the protection workflow taught by this module?

options.text: A Log Analytics workspace
options.explanation: Log Analytics stores monitoring logs, not this VM backup policy and recovery-point management entity.

options.text: An App Service deployment slot
options.explanation: A deployment slot stages a web app; it does not manage Azure VM backup recovery points.

options.text: A Recovery Services vault
options.explanation: Azure VM backup uses a Recovery Services vault to manage policies, recovery points and backup/restore operations.

options.text: An availability set
options.explanation: An availability set places VMs across failure domains and does not manage their backups.

questions.prompt: A team needs application-consistent backups of a Linux VM's application. What does the module require to capture application state appropriately?

options.text: Assume every Linux disk snapshot is automatically application-consistent
options.explanation: Filesystem or crash consistency is not the same as capturing application-consistent state.

options.text: Rely on Windows VSS writers running inside Linux
options.explanation: The module describes VSS for Windows and pre/post scripting for Linux applications.

options.text: Disable all backup policies
options.explanation: Disabling protection does not provide an application-consistent recovery point.

options.text: Suitable pre- and post-backup scripts for the application
options.explanation: Linux application consistency requires application-appropriate pre/post scripts; it should not be assumed from a basic snapshot alone.

questions.prompt: A protected VM has been deleted. An administrator wants to recover it from an available supported backup. Which statement about Replace existing is correct?

options.text: It cannot replace a deleted VM; use a supported new-VM or disk-restore path
options.explanation: Replace existing targets a VM that still exists. A deleted VM requires another supported restore option.

options.text: Replace existing automatically recreates any deleted VM
options.explanation: That is not the purpose or supported target of Replace existing.

options.text: Every backup becomes unusable when the source VM is deleted
options.explanation: A retained supported recovery point can be restored through appropriate new-VM or disk options.

options.text: Replace existing works once the deleted VM's old name is entered
options.explanation: A name does not restore the existing target required by Replace existing; use a supported new-VM or disk-restore path.

questions.prompt: An administrator wants recovered VM disks but needs to customize the new VM configuration rather than immediately recreate the original VM. Which restore option fits?

options.text: Replace existing on a production VM
options.explanation: Replace existing updates an existing VM's disks, rather than providing the requested separate customized recovery path.

options.text: Restore disk
options.explanation: Restore disk recovers disks and provides a template for customized VM creation; restored disks can also be attached where supported.

options.text: Create a new VM with no need to customize the recovered configuration
options.explanation: Create a new VM is the more direct recreation path; Restore disk matches the stated need to customize deployment from recovered disks.

options.text: Use file recovery instead of recovering disks
options.explanation: File recovery targets individual data items; the scenario asks for recovered VM disks for a customized deployment.

questions.prompt: A backup item is deleted accidentally while soft delete is enabled. What protection does soft delete provide?

options.text: It permanently deletes all recovery points immediately
options.explanation: Immediate permanent deletion is the opposite of the soft-delete protection.

options.text: It guarantees no administrator can ever delete backup data
options.explanation: Soft delete provides a retained recovery window, not an unlimited universal prohibition on deletion.

options.text: It retains deleted backup data for a recovery window
options.explanation: Soft delete preserves deleted backup data temporarily so it can be recovered within the configured protection period.

options.text: It changes the backup schedule to run more often
options.explanation: Soft delete retains deleted backup data; backup frequency is controlled separately by the backup policy.

questions.prompt: A newly created VM has host CPU graphs, but its guest event logs are needed for an investigation. Which configuration addresses the missing guest telemetry?

options.text: Wait for host metrics to become guest event logs automatically
options.explanation: Automatic host metrics do not replace configured guest event-log collection.

options.text: Configure only host CPU metric charts
options.explanation: Host CPU charts analyze host telemetry, not the requested guest event-log data source.

options.text: Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule for the required logs
options.explanation: Host metrics are automatic; guest event-log collection requires an agent and an appropriate DCR selecting data and destinations.

options.text: Use only boot diagnostics for routine guest event collection
options.explanation: Boot diagnostics provides startup screenshots/output; it does not replace a DCR for the requested guest event-log source.

questions.prompt: A Linux VM fails during startup. The administrator needs its boot screenshot and serial output. Which monitoring feature should they inspect?

options.text: Only a Metrics Explorer chart of Percentage CPU
options.explanation: CPU metrics can show resource use but do not provide the requested boot screenshot and serial output.

options.text: Only the Activity log of Azure resource operations
options.explanation: The Activity log records control-plane operations, rather than the guest boot screenshot and serial output.

options.text: Only the configured Syslog collection rule
options.explanation: Guest Syslog helps event investigation when collected, but Boot diagnostics is the feature for the requested startup screenshot and boot output.

options.text: Boot diagnostics
options.explanation: Boot diagnostics exposes screenshots and boot output for investigating startup failures.

questions.prompt: An administrator wants a chart that reveals the highest Percentage CPU value in each displayed time interval, rather than the average. Which aggregation matches?

options.text: Maximum
options.explanation: Maximum shows the highest sampled value in each aggregation interval, matching the request for peaks.

options.text: Average
options.explanation: Average smooths values across the interval instead of selecting the highest one.

options.text: Minimum
options.explanation: Minimum shows the lowest sampled value, not the peak.

options.text: Count
options.explanation: Count represents the number of measurements, not the highest CPU percentage.

questions.prompt: A team intentionally uses classic logs-based VM insights. Where are its predefined guest performance counters stored for the curated performance views?

options.text: An Azure Monitor workspace solely because OpenTelemetry is now the default
options.explanation: Azure Monitor workspaces store the OpenTelemetry metrics path; the scenario explicitly uses the classic logs-based path.

options.text: A Log Analytics workspace
options.explanation: Classic logs-based VM insights sends guest performance data to Log Analytics for its charts and workbooks.

options.text: A Recovery Services vault
options.explanation: A recovery vault manages backups, not this VM insights guest-performance dataset.

options.text: The VM Activity log
options.explanation: The Activity log records Azure resource operations; it is not the store for classic VM insights guest performance counters.

questions.prompt: A Linux VM needs Syslog events in a Log Analytics workspace. What should an administrator select in an additional data collection rule?

options.text: Only host Percentage CPU as the data source
options.explanation: CPU metrics do not capture the requested Syslog event records.

options.text: Only the predefined guest performance-counter rule
options.explanation: The performance rule is not a replacement for selecting the required guest event-log source.

options.text: Linux Syslog as the data source and the workspace as destination
options.explanation: The rule selects Linux Syslog and sends those guest events to the chosen Log Analytics workspace.

options.text: Select Windows event logs for the Linux Syslog requirement
options.explanation: Windows event logs are a different guest source; this Linux scenario specifically needs Syslog selected in its rule.

questions.prompt: After Syslog ingestion, an administrator wants to filter the records by severity in the VM Logs page. Which tool or language is appropriate?

options.text: A Metrics Explorer chart alone
options.explanation: Metrics Explorer plots numerical metric time series; the task asks to filter records already ingested into the Syslog log table.

options.text: Only the Azure Activity log
options.explanation: The Activity log concerns Azure resource operations, not the guest Syslog records selected for this investigation.

options.text: Only the Boot diagnostics screenshot
options.explanation: A boot screenshot helps startup diagnosis but does not query ingested Syslog records by severity.

options.text: A Kusto Query Language query against the Syslog table
options.explanation: KQL queries in Log Analytics can filter the collected Syslog records by relevant fields such as severity.
